title: What Is a Good Impact Factor for a Journal? | AnswerThis
summary: There is no single good impact factor. Compare a journal with others in its category by quartile. See how the number is calculated and what it misses.
body_markdown:
There is no single number that makes an impact factor good. A good impact factor is one that is high compared with other journals in the same subject category, and you check this with the quartile or percentile of the journal.


This guide shows how the number is calculated and why it differs by field. It also shows where to find it and what else to check before you choose a journal.


## TL;DR


-


An impact factor has meaning only inside its subject category.


-


Use the quartile. Q1 means the top 25 percent of journals in that category.


-


The Journal Impact Factor comes from Journal Citation Reports, which Clarivate publishes once a year.


-


The number describes a journal. It does not describe one article or one author.


-


Choose a journal for its scope and readers first. Look at metrics second.


## What is a good impact factor?


No cut-off works for every field. A value that is high in one subject can be ordinary in another.


Journal Citation Reports places each journal in one or more subject categories. It then ranks the journals inside each category by impact factor. Two figures show where a journal stands.


-


[Quartile](https://supportcenter.clarivate.com/s/article/Journal-Citation-Reports-Quartile-rankings-and-other-metrics?language=en_US) . The ranked list is split into four equal parts. Q1 is the top 25 percent and Q4 is the bottom 25 percent.


-


[Percentile](https://scimagojr.com/journalrank.php) . This places the journal on a scale from 0 to 100 within its category. A higher percentile means a higher rank.


So ask where the journal ranks in its category. That tells you more than the number alone.


## How is the Journal Impact Factor calculated?


The[Journal Impact Factor](https://clarivate.com/academia-government/download/journal-citation-reports-reference-guide/) is a ratio caclulated as follows:


*Journal Impact Factor = citations this year to items the journal published in the previous two years ÷ citable items the journal published in those two years*


Citable items are mainly research articles and reviews.


### Worked example


The journal in this example is invented.


1.


In 2023 and 2024, the journal published 200 citable items.


2.


In 2025, those items were cited 600 times.


3.


The 2025 impact factor is 600 ÷ 200 = 3.0.


An impact factor of 3.0 means that an item from those two years was cited three times on average in 2025. It is an average for the whole journal. Some articles get many more citations, and many get fewer.


The numbers run one year behind. The edition released in 2026 reports the 2025 impact factor.


## Why does the same impact factor mean different things in different fields?


Fields cite in different ways. Three things change the number.


-


Size of the field. More researchers and more papers produce more citations.


-


Speed of citation. The formula counts only two years. Fields where new papers are cited quickly get higher values.


-


Type of article. Journals that publish many reviews tend to collect more citations.


For this reason, an impact factor of 3 can place a journal in Q1 in one category and in a lower quartile in another. To compare journals from different fields, compare their quartiles or percentiles. Do not compare the raw numbers.


## How do you find the impact factor of a journal?


1.


Look in Journal Citation Reports. This is the official source. It needs a licence, and many university libraries provide access.


2.


Check the journal website. Many journals show the number on the home page or the About page. Confirm the year and that it is the Journal Impact Factor from Journal Citation Reports.


3.


Ask your librarian if you have no access.


The current edition is[Journal Citation Reports 2026](https://clarivate.com/news/clarivate-releases-journal-citation-reports-2026/) , released on 17 June 2026. It covers 22,643 journals in 254 categories.


AnswerThis[journal metrics checker](https://answerthis.io/impact-factor-checker) is free, with a rate limit. It shows the two-year mean citedness of a journal from OpenAlex and its article fee, each with a date. Two-year mean citedness is a different metric from the Journal Impact Factor. For the Journal Impact Factor and quartiles, use Journal Citation Reports.

## What can an impact factor not tell you?


-


The quality of one article. Citations inside a journal are highly skewed. A few articles receive most of them.


-


The quality of a researcher. Journal-based metrics should not be used to[judge](https://sfdora.org/read/) individual articles or scientists, or in hiring, promotion or funding decisions.


-


Whether the journal fits your paper. A high number does not help if the journal does not publish your topic.


Clarivate makes the same point. Its journal-level indicators are designed for evaluating journals, not individual researchers or articles.


## How do you choose a journal beyond the number?


Check these five things for every journal on your list.


1.


Scope. Does the journal publish your topic and your type of study?


2.


Readers. Will the people you want to reach read it?


3.


Indexing. Is it listed in the databases your field uses?


4.


Peer review. How long does a decision usually take?


5.


Fee. Is there an article processing charge, and can you pay it?


## Find journals that fit your paper


The AnswerThis[journal finder](https://answerthis.io/journal-finder) suggests journals from papers related to yours. Paste your abstract, or select Load example to see how it works. You get 3 free searches, and it draws on papers from 2016 onward. It does not screen for predatory practices, so check each journal yourself before you submit.


## FAQs


### Is an impact factor of 3 good?


It depends on the subject category. Check the quartile of the journal. A value of 3 can be Q1 in one category and lower in another.


### What is a Q1 journal?


A Q1 journal ranks in the top 25 percent of its subject category by impact factor.


### Is a higher impact factor always better?


No. A journal with a lower number can be the better choice if it fits your topic and reaches your readers.


### Do all journals have an impact factor?


No. Only journals covered in Journal Citation Reports have a Journal Impact Factor.


### How often is the impact factor updated?


Once a year. Each new edition of Journal Citation Reports reports the values for the previous year.


### What is the difference between impact factor and CiteScore?


They come from different databases and use different time windows. The impact factor uses two years of items. CiteScore uses four years.


### How do I compare impact factors across fields?


Compare the quartile or percentile of each journal within its own category. Raw impact factors from different fields are not comparable.
